item.title: Lasting Longer: What "Sexspan" Is and Why It Matters
item.description:
Sex

Lasting Longer: What "Sexspan" Is and Why It Matters

Prolonging our sex lives improves health and well-being.

Posted October 2, 2026

Key points
  • Good sex is good for your health.
  • Sexual activity is linked to both short- and long-term benefits.
  • Extending active sexuality into old age is challenging, but the benefits are worth it.

One need not stretch one’s imagination much to intuit that good sex is good for you, both in the moment and down the road. And research backs it up.

Source: RibhavAgrawal for Pixabay

For example, regarding the short term, a study by Yoobin Park of the University of California and colleagues (2024) analyzed two experience sampling datasets (N = 8,452) to examine changes in sleep, cardiovascular responses, and affect in the morning following sex. Their results showed both between-person associations, linking more positive daily health outcomes to more sexually active individuals, as well as within-person associations, suggesting that people regardless of gender or relationship status who had sex the previous night experienced better sleep quality, fewer sleep disturbances, lower blood pressure, less stress, more positive affect, and better coping in the morning.

It is also true in the long term. Sexual health is an important aspect of overall health, and sexual satisfaction is an important aspect of life satisfaction. Sex may help you live longer, especially if you consider this aspect of life important.

A 2022 study by Shanice Beerepoot and colleagues examined the association between sexuality and longevity and the factors that may shape the link. Using longitudinal data from a large (N=1,042) Dutch sample of middle aged and older adults, the researchers tracked sexual activity and survival for 27 years. Sixty percent of the participants reported their sexuality was enjoyable and 44 percent characterized it as important. Enjoyment of sexuality was positively associated with longevity, but only in those who perceived sexuality as important.

As with other aspects of health that relate to performance, the rule for sex is "use it or lose it." A key to having regular sex down the road is to have regular sex now. A 2025 study from Chinese urologist Mutong Chen, analyzing 15,794 U.S. adults ages 20–59, from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (2005–2016) found that sexual frequency of 1-2 times per week had the optimal effect in reducing depression and may be considered a benchmark for positive sexual and mental health.

Understanding and Improving Your "Sexspan"

The increasing interest in issues of sexuality and longevity has produced a new term, “sexspan,” coined by Dr. Mohit Khera, a urologist at Baylor College of Medicine to refer to prolonging sexual activity as far as possible into old age. Just as medicine has long been interested in prolonging people’s lives while retaining quality (aka “health span”), the concept of sexspan applies a similar approach to sexuality. The longer we can have good sex, the better, goes the (compelling) logic.

Not surprisingly, just as the recent interest in extending (maxxing) one’s health span and longevity appears to have intensified first among the super wealthy, so is the new interest in increasing the sexspan. Yet neither interest need remain exclusive to social higher ups. Good health and good sex are beneficial to all.

But how to go about improving your sexspan? Sex into old age requires addressing several distinct yet related domains of influence.

  1. Ageism and stigma: While sexual activity tends to persist into old age, our culture celebrates youthful sex and sexuality. Depictions and discussions of healthy, pleasurable sex among older people are scarce. Older adults interested in sex may often be depicted (and viewed) as creepy, predatory, pathetic, or unhinged. "Proper" elders are de-sexualized or viewed as uninterested in sexual activity. Consequently, older adults' sexual concerns are more readily ignored or dismissed. Physicians and other health professionals are often reluctant to inquire with older patients about their sexual health and enjoyment. Older people who wish to prolong their satisfying sex lives must resist internalizing societal stigma and remain proactive and assertive about maintaining their sexual health.
  2. Sex-specific concerns: Maintaining and enhancing sexual health and activity into old age requires different kinds of adaptations and interventions for men and women. Men often have to contend with erectile dysfunction, reduced testosterone levels, and the attendant psychological impact of performance anxiety. Women, for their part, must contend with the transition into menopause and the attendant hormonal and bodily changes, including reduced lubrication and vaginal atrophy, which may impact sexual desire and pleasure. Social expectations and pressure to remain young-looking create stress and may undermine self confidence. Older couples must communicate openly with each other and with their healthcare professionals about these challenges so as to address them effectively.
  3. Lifestyle choices: Sexual health, like health in general, depends in large part on our habits and choices. Here as elsewhere, trendy hacks and tricks are less likely to prove beneficial than the "usual suspects," for which ample evidence has accumulated: sleep well; eat food (as opposed to food products), exercise and move your body regularly; nurture your nurturing social connections; and manage stress.
  4. Partner issues: Most satisfying sex happens between mutually involved and attentive partners. Partnered sex involves more moving parts than solitary sex, and the parts, alas, are bound to show some wear and tear over time. Diseases and conditions prevalent or unique to old age (heart problems, arthritis, medication side effects, diabetes, incontinence, etc.) are bound to challenge one or both partners. Often, the frequency and quality of your sexual activity will depend in large part on the health and state of mind of your partner. Good communication is, as always, one important prerequisite, as sexual behaviors and expectations need to be recalibrated in light of the partners’ shifting abilities and concerns. What worked once may not work anymore. As physical flexibility decreases, psychological flexibility needs to increase. Adjustments must be made. A supportive partner will prove to be a major asset in the accommodative process of keeping the sex good and going.

item.title: AI Is Making Everyone's Ideas the Same
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

AI Is Making Everyone's Ideas the Same

AI makes your work easier. Yet it also makes you sound like everyone else.

Posted October 2, 2026

Key points
  • AI is slowly killing human creativity.
  • In today's world, you must rely on yourself to come up with great ideas.
  • Uniquely human qualities, like humor, empathy, and courage, can help people stand out amidst the AI slop.

If you pull up the last five proposals that landed on your desk, or the last five emails you sent, or that paper you were asked to write about market conditions, they may look slick. They may be polished. They may look focused, organized, and sophisticated.

You may even think that you are getting the hang of all this AI at work. And your confidence may be soaring. Yet something lies just beneath the surface.

Your work has never looked better, and it has never looked more alike. You can’t tell what your work is apart from what someone else’s work is. That’s the thing with AI.

AI makes everything look more or less the same.

My research has led me to a 2024 study in Science Advances: Anil Doshi of University College London and Oliver Hauser of the University of Exeter asked 300 people to write short stories.

Some got story ideas from AI, and some did not.

The AI-assisted stories were judged more creative, and the writers who started out least creative gained the most.

But here is the kicker: Those stories were also more similar to one another!

Not convinced yet? In a 2026 study in PNAS Nexus, Emily Wenger of Duke University and Yoed Kenett of the Technion-Israel Institute of Technology gave standard creativity tests to 22 AI models and more than 100 people.

The results? The models’ answers were far more alike than the people’s were.

Why does this happen? In 1974, legends Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman, then at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, showed in Science that the first number we see drags our judgment toward it.

They called it anchoring.

In their watershed experiment, people watched a wheel of fortune stop on a number, then estimated what percentage of United Nations members were African countries. When the wheel stopped on 10, the typical guess was 25 percent. When it stopped on 65, the typical guess was 45 percent.

The first answer “wins,” even when it is random.

Today AI hands millions of us the same first answer. The first anchor. It’s no wonder it drives us to slop and sameness.

But there is hope. Here are three things you can do to keep from conforming to everyone else’s ideas, and soar high above your AI-dependent peers:

1. See a World That Can Be

In my bestseller The Creator Mindset, I write about seeing a world that can be, not a world that is.

AI is built from the world that is. It has read what has already been written, and it hands you back the most likely version of it.

That is fine for a routine email.

It is a problem for an idea that is supposed to be yours.

So use this tip: before you open the AI chat window, write your own answer.

Three rough lines will do, and they are allowed to be bad. They should be bad! It’s a low-stakes exercise. Only then bring in AI to enhance your ideas.

Now that you have set the anchor, have the machine work for you, not the other way around.

2. Take a Chance

One of the tools in my new book The Solution Mindset is simple to say and hard to do: Take a chance.

It is hard because the safe choice is usually the one everyone else is making.

Michael Bar-Eli and his colleagues at Ben-Gurion University of the Negev and the Hebrew University of Jerusalem analyzed 286 penalty kicks from top soccer leagues in a 2007 study in the Journal of Economic Psychology.

A goalkeeper’s best chance of stopping the kick is to stay in the center of the goal.

Yet goalkeepers almost never do.

They dive left or right because diving is what goalkeepers are expected to do, and it’s exciting, and a penalty-scored goal just seems to hurt more when you simply stand still.

AI’s answer is the dive. Every time. Every way. Dive.

It is the expected move, the one nobody gets blamed for.

So when the options are on the table, ask which one would surprise people.

In this case, stay in the middle. Pick the one that could fail. Then test it small and cheap, so being wrong costs you a day or a week and not a year.

3. Lead With Humor, Empathy, and Courage

Another concept I use often is three traits most people never connect with creativity at work: humor, empathy, and courage.

They are also the three things a machine can’t bring from experience. And people can tell.

In 2025, Matan Rubin and Anat Perry of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, along with their colleagues, published nine studies with 6,282 people in Nature Human Behavior.

Participants read identical supportive messages. When they believed a human wrote the message, they rated it as more empathic and more supportive than when they believed AI wrote it.

The words were the same. The value was not.

So before anything leaves your desk, add one thing only you can make.

Handcraft it. Love it. Make it your own.

Maybe it’s a customer’s exact words. A joke or insight that could only come from your team. A position you are willing to defend out loud.

That is what turns the blah into wow.

At the end of the day, AI is making everyone’s creativity the same. Sure, it may look good at first, but the ever-present AI slop of the same results—the same thing over and over—demands that you come up with something different in order to stand out at work. And the three tools above are sure to give you that edge.

item.title: How to Reduce Harm and Increase Your Well-Being
item.description:
Environment

How to Reduce Harm and Increase Your Well-Being

Want to be kind to yourself and others? Open up to practicing compassion.

Posted October 2, 2026

Key points
  • Research shows that loving-kindness practices can promote wellness.
  • Compassion practice works across cultures.
  • A simple practice could help you cultivate compassion.

How can we possibly reduce harm? It's something I've been meditating on lately.

In particular, I've wondered how we can heal the blaming and shaming that seems to be dividing so many. One approach is practice compassion, or non-harm, towards others, which is a topic that has been talked about frequently throughout history by such persons as Gandhi, Martin Luther King, Jesus, and the Buddha.

Yes, the mystery of being is closer than you think!
Source: Amadeo-Valar/unsplash

Given how our world is infused with technology, you might be tempted to say that technology can provide the answer. Well, if that were the case, the world be experiencing an epidemic of love and kindness right now!

Here's the thing: Compassion is not an answer that is searched or found quickly by using a search engine or AI tool. Compassion is a practice that takes time. For example, the compassion practice I learned in the monastery many years ago is something I still practice today. It's invaluable, especially when I'm stressed or under a deadline.

It's worth remembering, too, that in today's world we are primed to make quick decisions. Technology offers quick information—which of course, is not the same as the experience and process of developing loving-kindness and compassion.

Any wisdom practices we apply get deepened as we mature over the course of a lifetime. Let's begin with a quote by Max Planck, the founder of quantum theory. He wrote:

"Science cannot solve the ultimate mystery of nature. And that is because, in the last analysis, we ourselves are part of nature and therefore part of the mystery that we are trying to solve."

A loving-kindness or compassion practice technology is incapable of doing. It invites us to experience the mystery of being by using our own consciousness and "beingness." When you think about that, it's brilliant—and it works across cultures, as shown in research that studied both Vietnamese and American employees. Researchers concluded, "The study provides robust evidence that compassion-based practices can serve as a universal, yet culturally adaptable, pathway to employee well-being."

Loving-kindness improves well-being because it helps us recognize that the world and all the living beings in it are not machines or pieces on a game board—to be moved around and manipulated. Instead, practitioners are steeped in the truth of how humans are intrinsically woven into the fabric of all things.

A Simple Compassion Practice

In some workshops, I've had people look into the eyes of someone they didn't know for up to three minutes in silence. This is not an easy thing to do, but many were stunned by the experience. Many persons shared how it was like looking in a mirror. They actually pictured themselves reflected in the other, which is the power of empathy.

Have you ever looked at someone, even an intimate friend or partner, for that long in silence? Probably not. (And I wouldn't advise it without proper guidance because even if you want to try it, the other person may not.)

Even though you may never try the above practice, you can still get the feeling of how to view others through the fresh eyes of compassion. These words from the Buddha speaks to this idea:

"See yourself in others.

All beings tremble before violence.

All fear death.

All love life.

See yourself in others.

Then whom can you hurt?

What harm can you do?"

Consider, too, that to some degree, we've lost the frequent caring and nurturing gaze of others, which links us to our ancestral thread. These days, it is computer devices and phones that often command our gaze.

Instead of peering deeply into the eyes of another person for several minutes, you can do the following as a simple practice:

  • Just be fully present with another while letting go any complaints you might have about the person's faults.
  • Imagine looking into the eyes of someone who you blame for various problems (locally or globally). Now, that person is no longer out of context, but is relatable, connected and part of your world.

Remember, too, that we are all part of the growing and adapting evolution of human-kind and human endeavors, like a thread stretching back thousands of years.

Conclusion

All is context and connection. Without context and without compassion and empathy for others, there is sure to be distortion, righteousness, pain, and suffering.

So we must ask: Can we move from the limited, machine-like fix it mentality—where all things are treated as lifeless objects? Is it possible? Could we cultivate a more spacious understanding and kindness for all living, breathing beings who share this planet with us?

We are in this together. Repeating the Buddha's advice and greeting others with openness, you show an open, kind heart and reduce harm for all of us. May we all spread seeds of kindness, compassion, and gratitude each day.

item.title: Detective Dogs’ Amazing Noses Can Sniff Out Invasive Species
item.description:
Animal Behavior

Detective Dogs’ Amazing Noses Can Sniff Out Invasive Species

Alison Pearce Stevens focuses on these dogs as accomplished conservationists.

Posted October 2, 2026

Key points
  • Dogs have amazing olfactory acuity; their noses are a great alternative to the broad use of nasty chemicals.
  • The dogs find that being conservationists is consistent with their desire for exercise and being outdoors.
Handler Josh and detective dog Dia inspect a rock wall for spotted lanternfly egg masses.
Source: Alison Pearce Stevens.

Invasive, or aggressively spreading non-native animal and plant species, present a major problem in ecosystems all over the world. Unfortunately, some attempts to locate and then remove these animals involve the use of different chemicals, including 1080 and others that also destroy ecosystems.

One solution is to take advantage of the amazing olfactory abilities of dogs and have them use their highly evolved, keen sense of smell to locate the unwanted intruders. These are among the reasons I found award-winning writer and behavioral ecologist Dr. Alison Pearce Stevens’s highly acclaimed new book Detective Dogs: How Working Dogs Sniff Out Invasive Species to be a fascinating read. Written for youngsters, it’s really a book for all ages.

Marc Bekoff: Why did you write Detective Dogs, and how did you come up with the title?

Alison Pearce Stevens: I’ve been concerned about the state of our natural spaces for a long time, so I’m drawn to topics that feature ways we can help the natural world. That’s especially true because I write for young people, and I want them to have hope for our future on this incredible planet.

A few years ago, I wrote an article about the role of dogs in conservation efforts. That story looked at how we can train dogs to sniff out all kinds of organisms that are otherwise difficult for people to find, from invasive species we’re trying to eradicate to elusive species we’re trying to protect. Dogs have even been trained to sniff out orca scat (not sure if scat is the right word—it’s a huge cloud of goop!) to help researchers study wild pods of orcas.

When the opportunity to write a book about these incredible canines arose, I jumped at it. I focused on invasive species, since they can wreak havoc on an ecosystem but are a group of organisms most young people don’t know much about. A book about invasive species probably wouldn’t grab most kids’ attention, but a book about those organisms told through the lens of sniffer dogs? That’s a completely different story.

As for the title, I’ve always loved mysteries. Science is a process of unraveling mysteries, and the subject matter seemed to fit within that framework, since it features dogs that are sniffing out conservation clues.

Source: Holiday House/with permission.

MB: How does your book relate to your background and general areas of interest?

APS: My background is in animal behavior and ecology, so this was a fun way to feature both of those things. Training the dogs requires a lot of positive reinforcement and playtime. Later, when dogs and their handlers are in the field, the dogs work hard to earn a few minutes of playtime with their favorite toy. Handlers have to pay close attention to their dog’s behavior, so they can pick up on subtle changes that indicate their dog has picked up a scent. And these teams are working to protect ecosystems that we rely on, so it all ties together.

MB: Who do you hope to reach?

APS: This book is for everyone: kids, adults, nature-lovers, dog-lovers. It’s written for upper elementary students, but it’s for adults, too. Animal lovers will enjoy learning about working dogs. People concerned about conservation will be interested to know how these dog-handler teams help protect those natural spaces. If you’ve ever had a boat checked for zebra mussels or dealt with a spotted lanternfly invasion, Detective Dogs provides information on why those animals pose a problem when they show up in new places and what people are doing about them.

MB: What are some of the topics you consider, and what are some of your major messages?

APS: I wanted to showcase the incredible relationships between the dogs and their handlers. They form tight bonds, and each relationship is unique (as are the dogs’ personalities!). That’s at the forefront of the story, which takes readers into the field with three different groups of dog-handler teams, each working in a unique location and environment.

I also wanted to provide deeper dives into some of the science behind conservation dog detective work. There are quite a few sidebars about invasive species: what makes them invasive, why the species featured in the book are problematic, and how humans play a role in both introducing species to new locations and stopping their spread. I always want my readers to feel empowered when they finish one of my stories, so the ending has information on what you need to know if you want to work with conservation dogs.

MB: How does your book differ from others that are concerned with some of the same general topics?

APS: I think a lot of people are familiar with sniffer dogs for search and rescue and other human-focused purposes. But in my experience, conservation dogs are less well-known. There are some other books written for the same age range that feature conservation dogs, but those tend to give an overview of all the various types of projects they work on. No other book takes an in-depth look at invasive species and why they cause so much trouble.

After a long day checking Snake River islands for invasive plants, Frost waits in the raft for the team to head home.
Source: Alison Pearce Stevens.

I accompanied each of the dog-handler teams profiled in the book, so I was able to drop readers into the field alongside the dogs. That allows readers to experience what it’s like to work in this area. For kids who are trying to figure out what they want to do when they grow up, it’s one more piece of information they can use to help make those decisions.

MB: Are you hopeful that as youngsters (and adults) learn more about these amazing dogs, they will come to appreciate how important they are for the ecological services they perform?

APS: Yes! Our ecosystems are really struggling, but they don’t get nearly as much attention as other pressing issues. I hope this book helps people understand how important these natural systems are. We are completely reliant on them, so it’s critical to protect them from additional damage and help them recover as much as we can.

The dogs play an essential role in that process. Their keen sense of smell allows them to find things people just can’t. Dogs’ abilities complement our own in some really extraordinary ways. We’re lucky to have such hard-working, loving, and dedicated companions!

item.title: How Does Debt Feel?
item.description:
Behavioral Economics

How Does Debt Feel?

The price of a coffee and the loss of “slack”

Posted October 2, 2026

Key points
  • Financial pressure turns small purchases into conscious trade-offs, costing precious mental space.
  • We often respond to scarcity by demanding more self-control, making the situation even more taxing.
  • Building good habits can protect our mental bandwidth by removing decisions we would otherwise have to make.

We tend to assume that the people who feel the financial squeeze are the ones who are actually broke. But you don’t need to be in debt to feel like you are. You only need to experience a loss of “slack.”

In systems design, “slack” is the buffer that allows things to absorb unexpected shocks without breaking. In personal finance, having slack means that you can always find enough pocket money for your purchases.

This is when most daily spending is friction-free and automatic. You buy a coffee, simply tap your phone; no worries about where the next latte comes from. The purchase consumes none of your working memory.

When slack evaporates, however, these automatic, harmless habits are instantly transformed into conscious trade-offs. Suddenly, buying a coffee is an active decision: If I spend five dollars here, what am I going to give up later this week?

Behavioral economists Sendhil Mullainathan and Eldar Shafir found that wealthier individuals, unsurprisingly, rarely think in terms of trade-offs for small purchases. They would often struggle to answer what they gave up to buy a five-dollar coffee, because the money came out of an abundant pool of slack. But a person under financial pressure can likely tell you exactly what they gave up: a bus ride home, a brand of cereal, or a few dollars toward the electricity bill.

This explains why an economic squeeze—like the recent cost-of-living crisis in the UK, where over 80 percent of adults reported a sudden rise in their daily expenses—feels so uniquely exhausting. For millions of households, a previously frictionless environment suddenly became a landscape of conscious, daily decisions.

Cognitive scientists have shown that holding competing trade-offs in one’s mind creates an inherently taxing load on working memory. We require “creative space” to come up with original ideas, solve complex problems, or just remain patient with mischievous kids at the dinner table. When every small choice requires decision-making bandwidth, it is with this exact mental space that we pay the price.

Enter the tunnel

To understand what happens to our creative space when slack disappears, it helps to look at how our mind manages our attention. In 1980, cognitive psychologist Michael Posner famously introduced the “spotlight model.” When everything is nice and normal, our attention operates like a floodlight, illuminating a wide, peripheral field of view. We can focus on our immediate work while simultaneously holding space for long-term goals, creative ideas, and future planning.

As financial pressure hits, however, we experience what’s called “cognitive tunneling.” Our brain switches from floodlight mode to a narrow spotlight. Inside the tunnel, we’re only focused on things that are directly related to the immediate crisis. A disproportionate share of our working memory is focused inward, toward solving a single, urgent question: How do I make it through this week?

In this state, our longer-term needs are heavily discounted. To an outside observer sitting comfortably with plenty of slack, taking out a high-interest payday loan looks like a lack of financial literacy. Or, indeed, if we turn down a job interview because we can’t afford to take an unpaid afternoon off work, we’ll get stuck in the lower-paying role forever.

In reality, a debt spiral is often driven by a series of perfectly logical choices. As environmental scientist Donella Meadows famously observed, a response that treats only the symptoms of a crisis often creates the conditions for the next crisis.

Reclaiming the headroom

Dealing with debt requires a holistic approach, because it’s both a day-to-day problem and a cognitive environment we need to manage.

When people living through an economic squeeze experience mental fatigue or a short temper, they often feel ashamed. But internalizing financial stress as a personal failure introduces a secondary cognitive tax; it wastes the exact working memory required to actually solve the problem. Recognizing that cognitive tunneling is a predictable biological response to scarcity rather than a character flaw is the first step toward conserving our mental bandwidth.

Relying on raw willpower to navigate an economic squeeze is a structural error, because willpower requires the very executive function that’s depleted by financial stress. A more effective approach is to design an environment that makes life easier.

This type of environment is especially important because the outside world is often actively fighting against us. Institutions—from credit card companies to government portals—frequently impose an administrative maze on people in financial distress, demanding immense executive function just to navigate forms, dodge late fees, or wait on hold to negotiate payment plans.

Because the system will not protect our cognitive bandwidth, we have to ruthlessly protect it ourselves. Staying under budget shouldn’t require exhausting mental arithmetic at the supermarket if a weekly grocery list eliminates the need for making decisions in the store. And maybe this is a good time to unsubscribe from all those “final offer” emails too.

Taking a break from breaking

Inside the tunnel, one’s natural instinct is to view leisure and mental peace as rewards reserved for later. But as systems theory shows, a system without slack cannot self-correct. If we wait until we are financially solvent to start protecting our mental space, we guarantee we will stay locked in short-term survival mode.

Carving out pockets of cognitive slack—a disconnected hour, a walk without a device, an evening where we strictly ignore our bank account—is not a reward. It is a necessary mechanism to cool the system down by providing just enough breathing room to spot long-term solutions or to recognize when it’s time to ask for professional help.

Ultimately, the true cost of debt is not just measured in cash; it is measured in a loss of attention. Money, in its most valuable form, acts as a buffer that protects our attention from being entirely consumed by survival.

item.title: Our Tribal Minds Can Badly Distort Our Perception of Reality
item.description:
Identity

Our Tribal Minds Can Badly Distort Our Perception of Reality

How ancient, evolved adaptations fuel modern political tension.

Posted October 2, 2026

Key points
  • Other people's views of reality, especially politics, can seem alien to us.
  • Evolutionary psychology holds clues to why people can perceive identical information radically differently.
  • Group identity, and unconsious needs for consonant beliefs about that identity, can drive our perceptions.

If you’re like me, you have friends or family members that don’t seem to inhabit the same planet that you do.

Despite being as educated as you, as intelligent as you, as experienced as you, with the same strong moral compass as you, some people close to you simply don’t perceive the political world the way you do.

If you are sitting with a friend watching news coverage of events like Jan 6, the Epstein files, the war with Iran or the latest political scandal, based upon your politics, the two of you might have entirely different takeaways from the same information. An event that is an obvious political witch hunt to you could look like powerful evidence of misconduct to your friend—or vice versa.

It might seem that modern political disagreements are rooted in contemporary events, but evolutionary psychology suggests that the origins of widely diverging views of reality go back much farther...

...to the stone age when homo sapiens lived in small groups of hunter gatherers.

Why our ancient brains think maintaining “tribal” identity is so important

Perception of politically charged news is driven by our individual politics, which are in turn part of our larger group identity (e.g. political party, race, gender).[5,6]

And our ancient, unconscious need to maintain a strong group identity can alter our perception of reality. Here’s why.

Evolutionary psychologists assert that many modern motivations grow out of ancient, deeply ingrained “evolved adaptations” that helped our ancestors thrive and survive in their tribes and clans, persist due to the slow pace of evolution relative to rapid changes in civilization and technology.[1]

Among the most important of evolved adaptations are those that help us thrive in groups, such as language, cheater detection, a theory of mind (understanding another’s motivation and intent) ability to interpret facial expressions and tone of voice, and, pertinent to this discussion, affinity group formation.[1]

Fitting into a group meant gaining access to scarce resources, better mate selection, and better opportunities for offspring The opposite was lso true: not fitting in risked ostracism and denial of crucial resources with potentially existential consequences [1]

And to fit in, a clear identity was required.

Maintaining a strong identity may not be as important as it was in ancient times, but our ancient brains don’t know that.

How identity drives perception

Because we innately need to maintain a strong sense of identity, when new information challenges the foundation of that identity, we feel what social psychologist Leon Festinger called cognitive dissonance, a collision between contradictory views or beliefs. [2]

For example, if we strongly identify with political party A, news that Party A’s leader committed a crime could create tension and discomfort, with an inner monologue that might say, “Party A are the good guys, but one of us did something bad, so maybe we’re not the good guys. Maybe I’m not a good guy.”

To avoid the discomfort and anxiety from that inner conflict, we reduce dissonance by adjusting our perception of the news from ‘My leader broke the law’ to… ‘That was an obvious political hit job.” Such a shift in perception would normally occur so swiftly (to protect our equanimity) that we wouldn’t even know we had made it [3,4] At a conscious level we’d simply think from the start ‘political hit job.’

Lab research reinforces this idea.

Giessner & van Knippenberg evaluated how followers judge a leader's effectiveness after a major failure or performance drop. [5]

They found that when a leader is perceived as an in-group prototypical leader (someone who strongly represents "us"), followers grant them a "license to fail". Followers evaluated a failing in-group leader as almost equally effective as a successful one. However, when a non-prototypical or out-group leader failed, their ratings plummeted. [5]

According to Giessner et al, followers attribute an in-group leader's mistakes to bad luck or situational factors, while attributing an out-group leader's identical mistakes to incompetence or bad intentions.[5]

What this means for you

The foregoing discussion implies that, if you strongly identify with a specific group, your perceptions of news and events that reflect on that group are bound to be distorted, just as perceptions of those in opposing groups are likely to be biased in the opposite direction.

Bear that in mind next time you sit on the couch watching the news with a friend of the opposite persuasion.

Their perception of reality may be distorted. But because both of your brains still live in the stone age--probably not more distorted than yours.

item.title: A Danger of AI Nobody Talks About
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

A Danger of AI Nobody Talks About

It's about how AI use is changing our free time.

Posted October 2, 2026

Key points
  • AI can disrupt the balance between trophy-oriented and process-oriented activities.
  • AI tends to highlight our human inadequacies, affecting our self-esteem.
  • AI's role in chores changes the way we use our free time but may lead to imbalance and dissatisfaction.

There is no shortage of dire warnings about the dangers of AI. In fact, these days the question is not so much whether AI will kill us all, but about just how it will do so. Climate catastrophe as a result of the energy use of data centers? Or AI superintelligence enslaving us and keeping us the way we now keep factory-grown chicken? I don’t intend to add to these apocalyptic horror scenarios.

Instead, I want to warn about a much less science-fiction-inspired, but more immediate and already salient psychological effect of recent developments in AI technology. It is that our attitude towards our free time has been changing.

It may be tempting to think that this is a good thing. AI does our annoying chores instead of us so that we can focus on those things that we really care about. AI does our taxes, proofreads our texts, and tells us which hotel or flight to book. So we don’t have to spend hours on this. As a result, we have much more free time to do what we really want.

But things are not so simple. AI is very good at achieving certain goals in the most efficient manner, and it does so much more quickly than we do. But life is not only about achieving goals. It is also about how we get there. It’s not always about the trophy. It’s also about the process.

In fact, there are two kinds of activities that we can call trophy activities and process activities. Some activities only make sense if they help you reach an endpoint or a goal. They are done in order to achieve something: moving to a new apartment, taking college entrance exams, or achieving some concrete hallmark of excellence, for example, getting tenure or winning a medal in a sports competition.

If you don’t achieve the end result, you have wasted your time. These are trophy activities. Winning an Olympic gold medal is peak trophy activity—the winner gets an actual trophy. But the “trophy” is often not made of gold. It may not even be an actual object; perhaps it’s something you can pontificate about on Facebook. We don’t do everything for the trophy, however. Some activities make sense even if there’s no end goal: walking along the beach, reading about something interesting, or just running for pleasure, not to beat the stopwatch.

Importantly, too much of either of these activities is a really bad idea. So we can talk about something like the trophy-process balance, on the analogy of the work-life balance. And while talk of the work-life balance can amount to little more than platitudes, maintaining a healthy trophy-process balance is of utmost importance.

And AI really messes with our trophy-process balance by taking away a lot of our trophy tasks. The result of this is not that we can now live in a bliss of only process activities. A life of exclusively process activities is not any better than a life of always going for the trophy. What we need is a healthy balance. In a life of exclusively process activities, we will soon miss process activities and the experience of achievement that comes with them.

But there is a final twist here. Any process activity will be much more difficult to find pleasure in, as it is hard not to compare our ability to achieve goals to that of AI systems, and in this respect we will always come up short. So there is a high psychological price we need to pay for the chores AI takes off our hands. It is a serious trophy-process imbalance, and the resolution of this imbalance is bound to leave us feeling inadequate.
